subject: HEALTH
overview: Plan about 20 minutes a day: a short reading or discussion, one hands-on activity (role-play, audit, log, chart), and a check question. The course builds the eight California health skills through units on mental and emotional health, relationships, bullying and online safety, injury prevention and first aid, emergency preparedness, violence prevention and personal safety, personal and consumer health, and community health, ending with an advocacy project. Preview sensitive weeks first — emotions and mental health (weeks 3–7, 16–17, including suicide-prevention resources), bullying and online predators (13–15), violence, weapons and grooming (26–27) — and keep conversations calm, factual and open. First-aid lessons are introductions only; consider a certified Red Cross or American Heart Association class for hands-on CPR training.

weeks.prep: Get a health journal and draw a wellness wheel with five slices (physical, emotional, social, intellectual, environmental). List the eight California health skills: essential concepts, analyzing influences, accessing valid information, interpersonal communication, decision making, goal setting, practicing health-enhancing behaviors, health promotion/advocacy. Write 12 behavior cards for sorting.
misconceptions: Thinking wellness is only physical. All five dimensions affect each other — poor sleep (physical) can cause irritability (emotional) and arguments (social).
Thinking a risk factor guarantees a bad outcome. Risk factors raise the chance of problems; protective factors lower it, and you can strengthen them.

days.guide: Your child rates each slice 1–5 and shades the wheel. Discuss the highest and lowest areas and how they connect.

questions.q: Give one example of a habit for intellectual and for environmental wellness.
questions.a: Intellectual: reading, learning a new skill, puzzles. Environmental: keeping your space clean, spending time outside, recycling.

days.guide: Your child matches the eight health skills to middle-school scenarios and writes one example of each.

questions.q: A student checks whether a supplement ad is trustworthy by looking at the CDC website. Which skill is that?
questions.a: Accessing valid information.

days.guide: Your child sorts 12 behaviors (e.g., wearing a helmet, skipping breakfast, having a trusted adult, vaping) into risk or protective factors and explains two.

questions.q: Is 'being involved in a sport or club' a risk or protective factor? Why?
questions.a: Protective — it builds skills, positive friendships and supervised time, lowering the chance of risky behavior.

days.guide: Your child writes a SMART goal for the lowest wheel section and makes a tracker. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Rewrite as a SMART goal: 'I'll be more social.'
questions.a: Example: 'I will call or meet a friend at least twice a week for the next 4 weeks and log it on my tracker.'

days.guide: Give a quick check orally; your child shares the goal with you. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Name the five dimensions of wellness on the wheel.
questions.a: Physical, emotional, social, intellectual, environmental.

weeks.assessment_key: Quick check key: 1) five dimensions — physical, emotional, social, intellectual, environmental 2) dimensions affect each other (example) 3) risk factor = raises chance of harm; protective factor = lowers it 4) one example of each 5) SMART = Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. SMART goal rubric: 4 = all SMART parts, targets lowest area, includes tracker; 3 = one part missing; 2 = vague; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Computer access. Print a source checklist (CRAAP: Currency — when written? Relevance — answers my question? Authority — who wrote it, credentials? Accuracy — supported by evidence? Purpose — inform or sell?). Find three sources on one topic (e.g., sleep for teens): a .gov page, a health blog, and an influencer video.
misconceptions: Thinking popular means accurate. Likes and followers don't measure accuracy; check credentials and evidence.
Thinking the first option you think of is the only one. DECIDE asks you to explore several options before choosing.

days.guide: Teach DECIDE: Define the problem, Explore options, Consider consequences, Identify values, Decide and act, Evaluate. Apply to staying up late to finish a show on a school night.

questions.q: In DECIDE, what does the 'I' step ask you to do?
questions.a: Identify your values — think about what matters to you (health, family rules, goals) and how each option fits them.

days.guide: Your child rates the three sources on each CRAAP item and ranks them. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Why is an influencer video often less reliable than a .gov page?
questions.a: The influencer may not have health credentials, may be paid to promote products, and may not cite evidence; government health sites are written by experts and reviewed.

days.guide: Find two online health claims (e.g., a detox tea, a supplement); your child identifies who profits.

questions.q: How does making money from a product create bias?
questions.a: The seller benefits if you buy, so they may exaggerate benefits and hide risks.

days.guide: Apply DECIDE to a friend daring your child to jump off a high wall. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What are two options besides jumping, and their consequences?
questions.a: Say no and suggest something else (stay safe, friend may tease briefly); walk away (stay safe). Jumping risks broken bones or a head injury.

days.guide: Your child evaluates a new health website in writing and takes a 6-question quiz. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: What does 'credentials' mean?
questions.a: Qualifications such as a medical degree or expertise showing someone knows the subject.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) DECIDE steps in order 2) valid source = expert, current, evidence-based, unbiased 3) bias = slant from personal gain 4) .gov/.edu/medical organizations usually reliable 5) check the author's credentials 6) evaluate = reflect on the outcome. Website evaluation: 4 = addresses all five CRAAP criteria with evidence and a justified verdict; 3 = four criteria; 2 = two or three; 1 = one or none.

weeks.prep: Print a feelings wheel and a body outline; set up two journal pages for trigger tracking. PARENT PREVIEW: read the materials first; if your child shares feelings that worry you (hopelessness, self-harm, not wanting to live), stay calm, listen, and contact your pediatrician or the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988).
misconceptions: Thinking some emotions are 'bad.' All emotions are normal signals; what matters is how we respond.
Thinking emotions come out of nowhere. Most have triggers and body cues you can learn to notice early.

days.guide: Your child finds 15 emotions beyond happy/sad/mad (e.g., frustrated, jealous, proud, anxious, lonely) and writes a situation for each.

questions.q: Why is it helpful to name emotions precisely?
questions.a: Naming a feeling clearly ('frustrated' vs. 'mad') helps you understand it and choose the right way to handle it.

days.guide: Your child maps where anger, anxiety and excitement show in the body (hot face, tight fists, racing heart, butterflies).

questions.q: What are body cues?
questions.a: Physical signs of an emotion, like a racing heart, tense muscles or a hot face.

days.guide: Track triggers in a journal for two days (what happened, emotion, body cue, response). Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What is an emotional trigger?
questions.a: An event or situation that sets off a strong emotion.

days.guide: Sort responses to anger (yelling, hitting, deep breaths, walking away, talking it out) into healthy and unhealthy; role-play two healthy ones.

questions.q: Give two healthy ways to express anger.
questions.a: Take deep breaths, walk away to cool down, use an I-message, exercise, write about it.

days.guide: Your child writes a journal entry analyzing one emotion, its trigger and response. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What is emotional regulation?
questions.a: Managing your emotions so you respond in healthy, helpful ways.

weeks.assessment_key: Check key: emotions are normal; triggers set them off; body cues warn us; healthy expression examples; empathy = understanding others' feelings. Journal analysis: 4 = names specific emotion, trigger, body cue, response and a better alternative if needed; 3 = three elements; 2 = two; 1 = one.

weeks.prep: Print a fight-or-flight diagram, a stress inventory (list of common middle-school stressors with ratings 0–3), and 10 situation cards. Have a timer for pulse checks.
misconceptions: Thinking all stress is bad. Eustress (positive stress) can motivate, like before a game or performance.
Thinking stress is only in your head. Stress causes real body changes (hormones, heart rate, muscle tension).

days.guide: Explain fight-or-flight: adrenaline and cortisol are released; heart rate and breathing speed up, muscles tense, pupils widen, digestion slows. Your child labels the diagram.

questions.q: Which hormones are released in the stress response?
questions.a: Adrenaline (epinephrine) and cortisol.

days.guide: Your child classifies 10 situations (big game, test, moving, a fight with a friend, starting a new club) as eustress or distress.

questions.q: What's the difference between eustress and distress?
questions.a: Eustress is positive stress that motivates (a performance); distress is negative stress that harms or overwhelms (ongoing conflict).

days.guide: Complete the stress inventory; identify top three stressors. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What is a stressor?
questions.a: Anything that causes stress.

days.guide: Read about long-term stress effects on sleep, immunity and concentration. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: How can long-term stress affect health?
questions.a: It can disrupt sleep, weaken the immune system, cause headaches/stomachaches and make it hard to concentrate.

days.guide: Take the stress-concepts quiz. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: Why did the fight-or-flight response develop?
questions.a: To help people react quickly to danger by fighting or running away.

weeks.assessment_key: Stress quiz key: 1) stress = body's response to demands 2) stressor 3) eustress vs distress 4) fight-or-flight effects 5) adrenaline/cortisol 6) long-term effects: sleep, immunity, concentration. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Have a timer, planner, and a progressive muscle relaxation script (many free scripts online). Box breathing: in 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4. 4-7-8 breathing: in 4, hold 7, out 8.
misconceptions: Thinking coping means avoiding problems. Healthy coping manages stress so you can face the problem.
Using only one strategy. Different situations need different tools.

days.guide: Take pulse; practice box breathing and 4-7-8 breathing for 2 minutes each; retake pulse. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Why does slow breathing lower stress?
questions.a: It activates the body's relaxation response, slowing heart rate and calming the nervous system.

days.guide: Follow a progressive muscle relaxation script: tense each muscle group for 5 seconds, then release.

questions.q: How does progressive muscle relaxation work?
questions.a: Tensing then releasing muscles helps you notice and let go of tension.

days.guide: Plan the coming week in a planner, blocking schoolwork, activity, chores and rest. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: How does time management reduce stress?
questions.a: Planning prevents last-minute rushing and shows when there's time for rest.

days.guide: Build a coping toolbox of 8 strategies. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Name four healthy coping strategies.
questions.a: Exercise, music, talking to someone, art, time in nature, deep breathing, journaling.

days.guide: Write a personal stress-management plan; use one strategy daily for a week. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What should a stress-management plan include?
questions.a: Top stressors, specific coping strategies for each, and a trusted adult to talk to.

weeks.assessment_key: Plan rubric: 4 = names top stressors, matches specific strategies to each, includes time management and a support person, plus a daily log; 3 = missing one; 2 = vague; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Index cards and the health journal. Find a short article on growth mindset/brain plasticity and a biography excerpt of someone who overcame adversity (e.g., Wilma Rudolph, Malala Yousafzai, Temple Grandin).
misconceptions: Thinking self-esteem means thinking you're perfect. Healthy self-esteem means valuing yourself while accepting mistakes.
Thinking abilities are fixed. The brain grows with effort and practice (growth mindset).

days.guide: List 10 strengths; ask a family member to add three. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Why is it helpful to know your strengths?
questions.a: It builds confidence and helps you use strengths to handle challenges.

days.guide: Rewrite 6 negative self-talk statements as realistic positive ones. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Rewrite: 'I'm terrible at math.'
questions.a: 'Math is hard for me right now, but I can improve with practice and help.'

days.guide: Read the growth-mindset article; write about something improved with effort. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What is a growth mindset?
questions.a: The belief that abilities can grow through effort, practice and learning from mistakes.

days.guide: Read the biography excerpt; identify resilience traits (persistence, support, optimism, problem-solving).

questions.q: What is resilience?
questions.a: The ability to bounce back from difficulty.

days.guide: Set a mental-health goal; complete the check. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Give an example of a mental-health goal.
questions.a: 'I will write three things I did well each night for two weeks.'

weeks.assessment_key: Check key: self-esteem = how you value yourself; growth mindset = abilities grow with effort; positive self-talk example; resilience = bouncing back; one resilience trait. Goal: SMART and related to mental health.

weeks.prep: Print a screen-time and mood log (time, app, minutes, mood before/after). Gather magazines or screenshots showing filtered images. Read about how recommendation algorithms work (Common Sense Media has teen-friendly explanations). Find the AAP Family Media Plan tool (healthychildren.org). PARENT PREVIEW: read the materials first; if your child shares feelings that worry you (hopelessness, self-harm, not wanting to live), stay calm, listen, and contact your pediatrician or the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988).
misconceptions: Thinking social media shows real life. Posts are curated highlights, often edited or filtered.
Thinking you're in full control of how long you scroll. Apps are designed (infinite scroll, autoplay, notifications) to keep you using them.

days.guide: Discuss curated posts and the comparison trap; your child lists three edited-reality examples (filters, posed photos, only showing highlights).

questions.q: Why can scrolling social media make people feel worse about themselves?
questions.a: They compare their real everyday life to others' edited highlight reels.

days.guide: Your child logs screen use and mood for two days and looks for patterns. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What pattern might you find in a screen-time and mood log?
questions.a: Example: feeling more tired or down after long scrolling, or better after video-chatting a friend.

days.guide: Explain that algorithms track what you watch and show more of it; identify design features (infinite scroll, autoplay, likes, streaks, notifications).

questions.q: Name two design features that keep users scrolling.
questions.a: Infinite scroll, autoplay, notifications, streaks, likes.

days.guide: Write a family media plan with screen-free times (meals, an hour before bed) and zones (bedrooms).

questions.q: Why keep devices out of bedrooms at night?
questions.a: Screens and notifications delay sleep and reduce sleep quality.

days.guide: Give the Emotions and Stress unit test. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: What does FOMO stand for, and how can you manage it?
questions.a: Fear of missing out; take breaks from social media, focus on real-life activities and remember posts are highlights.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit test key: 1) feelings wheel/naming emotions 2) triggers and body cues 3) healthy vs. unhealthy expression 4) fight-or-flight (adrenaline, cortisol) 5) eustress vs. distress 6) two breathing techniques 7) coping strategies 8) growth mindset and resilience 9) positive self-talk 10) social media comparison/algorithms. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Write scenario cards for friendship behaviors and boundary role-plays (a friend copies your homework, shares your secret, pressures you to skip practice). Draw a spectrum chart from healthy to unhealthy.
misconceptions: Thinking a 'real friend' never disagrees. Healthy friends can disagree respectfully.
Thinking setting boundaries is mean. Boundaries protect both people and keep friendships healthy.

days.guide: Your child ranks 12 friendship qualities (trust, loyalty, humor, honesty, kindness...) and explains the top three.

questions.q: Why is trust important in a friendship?
questions.a: It lets you share feelings and rely on each other without fear of being hurt or betrayed.

days.guide: Sort behaviors (support, gossip, exclusion, honesty, control, jealousy, encouragement) on the spectrum chart.

questions.q: Where does 'telling you who you can't hang out with' belong?
questions.a: Unhealthy — it's controlling behavior.

days.guide: Role-play setting a boundary in 3 scenarios with a calm, clear statement. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Give an example of setting a boundary.
questions.a: 'I'm not comfortable sharing my homework. I can help you understand the problem instead.'

days.guide: Plan ways to make new friends (clubs, sports, co-ops, volunteering) and conversation starters.

questions.q: Name two ways to meet new friends.
questions.a: Join a club or team, volunteer, attend co-op classes, invite someone to do an activity.

days.guide: Write a letter about the friend you want to be; complete the check. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What is manipulation in a friendship?
questions.a: Trying to control someone through guilt, pressure, lies or threats.

weeks.assessment_key: Check key: healthy friendship qualities (trust, respect, honesty, support); unhealthy signs (control, gossip, exclusion, manipulation); boundary definition. Letter rubric: 4 = names 3+ qualities with examples of actions; 3 = qualities with some examples; 2 = list only; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Write scenario cards (someone cuts in line; a sibling borrows something without asking). Have a mirror. I-message formula: I feel ___ when ___ because ___. I need ___.
misconceptions: Thinking assertive means aggressive. Assertive is firm and respectful; aggressive attacks or blames.
Thinking listening means waiting to talk. Active listening means focusing, then paraphrasing what you heard.

days.guide: Act out passive, aggressive and assertive responses to the same situation; compare. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Someone cuts in line. Give an assertive response.
questions.a: 'Excuse me, I was in line first. Please go to the back.'

days.guide: Rewrite 6 blaming statements as I-messages. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Rewrite: 'You always ruin everything!'
questions.a: 'I feel frustrated when my project gets knocked over because I worked hard on it. I need you to be careful around my desk.'

days.guide: Practice paraphrasing in a 5-minute conversation. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What is paraphrasing?
questions.a: Restating what someone said in your own words to show you understood.

days.guide: Practice assertive body language and tone in a mirror. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Describe assertive body language.
questions.a: Stand tall, eye contact, calm steady voice, relaxed hands.

days.guide: Perform an assertive role-play scored with a rubric. Treat it like a real event: quiet audience, a short spoken introduction and a bow; then debrief together using the week's rubric, starting with what went well.

questions.q: Why do I-messages reduce conflict?
questions.a: They express feelings without blaming, so the other person is less defensive.

weeks.assessment_key: Communication rubric (1–4 each): uses an I-message with all parts; assertive tone and body language; listens and paraphrases; reaches a respectful outcome. Proficient = 3+ each.

weeks.prep: Print a conflict-resolution steps chart: 1) Cool down 2) Take turns telling your side 3) Listen and paraphrase 4) Brainstorm solutions 5) Agree on a win-win 6) Follow up. Write a scripted peer conflict for mediation.
misconceptions: Thinking conflict is always bad. Conflict is normal and can be solved in ways that strengthen relationships.
Thinking someone must win. Win-win solutions meet both people's needs.

days.guide: List common causes of conflict (misunderstandings, jealousy, sharing, rumors, different opinions).

questions.q: Name three common causes of conflict.
questions.a: Misunderstandings, rumors/gossip, competing for the same thing, different values, jealousy.

days.guide: Teach the six steps. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Why is cooling down the first step?
questions.a: When emotions are high, people say hurtful things; calm minds solve problems better.

days.guide: Role-play a sibling or friend conflict using the steps. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What is a compromise?
questions.a: Each person gives up something to reach an agreement.

days.guide: Your child mediates a scripted conflict. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What does a mediator do?
questions.a: A neutral person who helps others talk and find a solution without taking sides.

days.guide: Write a solution for a new scenario using every step. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What is a win-win solution?
questions.a: A solution where both people get their needs met.

weeks.assessment_key: Written solution rubric: 4 = all six steps applied specifically, with a realistic win-win; 3 = five steps; 2 = three or four; 1 = fewer.

weeks.prep: Write peer-pressure scenario cards (direct: 'Come on, just try it'; indirect: everyone wearing a brand; online: a group chat dare). Prepare interview questions about family roles.
misconceptions: Thinking peer pressure is always negative. Positive peer pressure encourages good choices.
Thinking family communication just happens. Family meetings and I-messages help.

days.guide: Identify direct, indirect and online pressure. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Give an example of indirect peer pressure.
questions.a: Feeling you must buy certain shoes because everyone has them, though no one asked.

days.guide: Write examples of positive peer pressure. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Give an example of positive peer pressure.
questions.a: A friend encouraging you to join a team or study for a test.

days.guide: Interview a family member about responsibilities and communication. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Why do families have roles and responsibilities?
questions.a: To share work, support each other and keep the household running.

days.guide: Lead a family meeting using I-messages to plan an activity. Set up a simple 'stage' and audience, have your child introduce the work, and hold applause until the end; afterward ask them to name one strength and one thing to improve before you add one specific comment.

questions.q: What makes a family meeting effective?
questions.a: Everyone gets a turn, uses respectful language, and agrees on a plan.

days.guide: Take the Relationships unit test. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: What is active listening?
questions.a: Focusing fully on the speaker and paraphrasing what they said.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit test key: healthy vs. unhealthy friendship traits; boundaries; passive/aggressive/assertive; I-message parts; active listening; conflict-resolution steps; mediator; win-win; types of peer pressure (direct, indirect, online); positive peer pressure. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Find picture books or articles about inclusion (e.g., 'Wonder' excerpt, 'The Day You Begin'). Gather 5 media examples showing stereotypes.
misconceptions: Thinking stereotypes are harmless if they're 'positive.' Any stereotype ignores individuals and can hurt.
Thinking being 'nice' is enough. Inclusion means actively welcoming people.

days.guide: Create an identity map; compare with a family member's. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What is identity?
questions.a: The qualities, background and beliefs that make you who you are.

days.guide: Identify stereotypes in 5 media examples; explain harm. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: What is a stereotype?
questions.a: An oversimplified belief that all members of a group are the same.

days.guide: Read a story about exclusion; rewrite the ending to show inclusion. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What does inclusion look like?
questions.a: Inviting others, making room, listening and valuing differences.

days.guide: List ways to include people with disabilities, new students or different family structures.

questions.q: How can you include a new student?
questions.a: Introduce yourself, invite them to sit with you, show them around.

days.guide: Write a paragraph on how respect supports mental health; complete the check. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What's the difference between prejudice and discrimination?
questions.a: Prejudice is an unfair judgment or attitude; discrimination is unfair treatment or action.

weeks.assessment_key: Check key: diversity, stereotype, prejudice (attitude), discrimination (action), inclusion. Paragraph rubric: 4 = explains how respect/inclusion improves belonging and mental health with examples; 3 = explanation without examples; 2 = vague; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Print materials from StopBullying.gov. Write 8 scenarios mixing bullying and ordinary conflict. PARENT PREVIEW: ask whether your child has experienced or witnessed bullying; listen without overreacting.
misconceptions: Calling every disagreement bullying. Bullying is unwanted aggressive behavior with a power imbalance that is repeated or likely to be repeated; a one-time argument between equals is conflict.
Thinking bystanders have no role. Bystanders can become upstanders by safely helping or reporting.

days.guide: Your child classifies 8 scenarios as bullying or conflict, citing repetition and power imbalance.

questions.q: Two friends argue once about a game. Bullying or conflict?
questions.a: Conflict — it's a one-time disagreement between equals.

days.guide: Chart physical, verbal, social/relational and cyber bullying with examples and effects. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Give an example of social (relational) bullying.
questions.a: Spreading rumors, deliberately excluding someone, or turning friends against them.

days.guide: Learn bystander, upstander and reporter roles; practice safe upstander responses. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Name two safe ways to be an upstander.
questions.a: Don't join in or laugh, invite the targeted person to leave with you, say 'That's not cool,' or tell a trusted adult.

days.guide: Write a script for reporting bullying to a trusted adult. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What should you include when reporting bullying?
questions.a: Who was involved, what happened, when and where, how often, and any evidence such as screenshots.

days.guide: Complete the bullying scenario quiz. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: What is a power imbalance?
questions.a: When one person has more power (size, popularity, numbers, information) than the other.

weeks.assessment_key: Scenario quiz key: bullying = unwanted, aggressive, power imbalance, repeated; four forms: physical, verbal, social, cyber; upstander actions; reporting to a trusted adult; telling is not tattling when someone is being hurt. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Preview a Common Sense Education digital citizenship lesson (grade 6, free). Sit with your child to review privacy settings on a family device or app. Write 5 sample messages (phishing, prize scam, stranger asking for photos, a real message, a friend request from someone unknown).
misconceptions: Thinking deleted posts disappear. Screenshots, archives and shares can keep them forever.
Thinking online strangers are always obvious. Predators may pretend to be kids and build trust slowly.

days.guide: Discuss a made-up name scenario: what a search could reveal (photos, comments, school) and how long it lasts.

questions.q: What is a digital footprint?
questions.a: The trail of information you leave online, which can be permanent and seen by others.

days.guide: Review privacy settings with a parent: private account, location off, who can message you.

questions.q: Why turn off location sharing?
questions.a: So strangers can't find where you are or live.

days.guide: Identify red flags in 5 messages. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Name three red flags of a phishing or scam message.
questions.a: Urgent demands, requests for passwords or personal info, prizes you didn't enter, misspellings, strange links or senders.

days.guide: Role-play refusing and reporting an online stranger who asks for photos or to meet. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What should you do if an online stranger asks for a photo or to meet?
questions.a: Don't respond or share, screenshot, block, and tell a trusted adult right away.

days.guide: Complete a Common Sense lesson and quiz. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: What information should you never share online?
questions.a: Full name with address, phone number, school, passwords, location, or private photos.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: digital footprint is permanent; private settings; scam red flags; never share personal info; stop-block-tell for strangers; think before you post. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Gather poster paper, markers or a video app. Review the Stop–Screenshot–Block–Tell response.
misconceptions: Replying to a cyberbully to defend yourself. Replying often escalates it; save evidence, block and tell.
Thinking online cruelty is less harmful. Cyberbullying can reach a large audience, is permanent and can happen anytime.

days.guide: Analyze how cyberbullying differs: larger audience, permanence, anonymity, 24/7. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Name two ways cyberbullying differs from in-person bullying.
questions.a: It can reach a huge audience, stays online permanently, can be anonymous, and happens any time.

days.guide: Practice: don't reply, screenshot, block, tell a trusted adult. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Why take a screenshot before blocking?
questions.a: It saves evidence to show adults or report to the platform.

days.guide: Design a kindness or anti-bullying poster or short video. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What makes an anti-bullying message effective?
questions.a: A clear positive message, specific actions people can take, and an appealing design.

days.guide: Share the campaign with family or co-op. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What is advocacy?
questions.a: Speaking up to encourage healthy behaviors or support a cause.

days.guide: Take the Respect and Bullying Prevention unit test. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: What should you do if you see someone cyberbullied?
questions.a: Don't share or like it, support the target, report it, and tell a trusted adult.

weeks.assessment_key: Campaign: clear message, accurate info, call to action. Unit test key: stereotype/prejudice/discrimination; inclusion; bullying definition and forms; upstander; digital footprint; scam red flags; stop-screenshot-block-tell. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Read KidsHealth teen articles on depression and anxiety. Draw a continuum line (thriving – surviving – struggling – in crisis). PARENT PREVIEW: read the materials first; if your child shares feelings that worry you (hopelessness, self-harm, not wanting to live), stay calm, listen, and contact your pediatrician or the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988).
misconceptions: Thinking mental illness is a weakness or choice. It's a health condition, like asthma, that can be treated.
Thinking feeling sad sometimes means depression. Depression is lasting (two weeks or more) and affects daily life.

days.guide: Place examples on the continuum. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Can someone move along the mental health continuum?
questions.a: Yes — mental health changes over time, and support and treatment help people move toward thriving.

days.guide: Read articles; list warning signs of depression and anxiety. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Name three warning signs of depression.
questions.a: Lasting sadness or irritability, losing interest in activities, sleep or appetite changes, low energy, trouble concentrating, feeling hopeless.

days.guide: Discuss myths and rewrite them as facts. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Rewrite the myth: 'People with mental illness can just snap out of it.'
questions.a: Fact: Mental illness is a health condition; people need support and often treatment, not willpower alone.

days.guide: Learn about counseling and treatment; why early help matters. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Why does getting help early matter?
questions.a: Treatment works better early and prevents problems from getting worse.

days.guide: Signs-and-symptoms matching check. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Name two signs of an anxiety disorder.
questions.a: Constant worry, racing heart, trouble sleeping, avoiding situations, stomachaches.

weeks.assessment_key: Matching check: depression — lasting sadness, loss of interest, hopelessness, sleep/appetite change; anxiety — excessive worry, restlessness, racing heart, avoidance; stigma = negative attitudes; treatment = counseling, therapy, sometimes medicine. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Make a resource card template. Know local resources: pediatrician, school or co-op counselor, county mental health line; 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988); Crisis Text Line (text HOME to 741741); 911 for immediate danger. PARENT PREVIEW: read the materials first; if your child shares feelings that worry you (hopelessness, self-harm, not wanting to live), stay calm, listen, and contact your pediatrician or the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988).
misconceptions: Promising to keep a friend's dangerous secret. If someone might hurt themselves or others, you must tell a trusted adult.
Thinking asking about suicide puts the idea in someone's head. Asking directly and caring is safe and helps.

days.guide: List school, community and crisis resources including 988. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What is 988?
questions.a: The Suicide & Crisis Lifeline — call or text 988 any time for free, confidential support.

days.guide: Learn: notice, ask, listen, tell a trusted adult. Practice with a scenario. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: A friend says 'Nothing matters anymore.' What do you do?
questions.a: Take it seriously, ask how they're feeling, listen without judging, and tell a trusted adult right away.

days.guide: Discuss why some secrets must be shared. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: When should you break a promise to keep a secret?
questions.a: When someone could be hurt—if they talk about hurting themselves or others, or are being hurt.

days.guide: Write a personal self-care plan for hard days. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What belongs in a self-care plan?
questions.a: Coping strategies, people to talk to, healthy activities, and crisis numbers.

days.guide: Create a resource card and take the Mental Health unit quiz. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: Who can be a trusted adult?
questions.a: A parent, relative, counselor, teacher, coach, doctor or faith leader.

weeks.assessment_key: Resource card: 988, 911, a trusted adult's number, a counselor/doctor. Unit quiz key: continuum, warning signs, stigma, treatment works, notice-ask-listen-tell, safety secrets must be shared, 988. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Print a home safety checklist (smoke and CO alarms on each level and near bedrooms, tested monthly; cords; chemicals stored high and locked; stairs clear; medicines secured). Find CDC injury data for ages 10–14 (WISQARS). Have a flashlight. Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222.
misconceptions: Thinking injuries are 'accidents' that can't be prevented. Most injuries are predictable and preventable.
Mixing cleaning chemicals to clean better. Mixing bleach and ammonia creates toxic gas.

days.guide: Read injury data; graph the top five causes. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What is the leading cause of injury death for kids 10–14?
questions.a: Motor vehicle crashes (falls and being struck by objects cause many non-fatal injuries).

days.guide: Do a home safety audit with a parent. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: How often should smoke alarms be tested?
questions.a: Monthly (and batteries replaced as needed).

days.guide: List rules for preventing burns and cuts; practice safe stove use. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Why turn pot handles inward?
questions.a: So no one bumps or grabs them and spills hot food.

days.guide: Check chemical storage; post Poison Control. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why should chemicals stay in original containers?
questions.a: So they're labeled with ingredients and warnings and not mistaken for drinks or food.

days.guide: Write a home safety action plan. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What does carbon monoxide do and why need a CO alarm?
questions.a: CO is an invisible, odorless poison gas that stops blood carrying oxygen; an alarm detects it.

weeks.assessment_key: Home safety plan: lists hazards found, specific fixes, who will do them, when. Check key: smoke/CO alarms tested monthly; chemicals stored safely; never mix bleach and ammonia; Poison Control 1-800-222-1222; pot handles in. Proficient = 4/5.

weeks.prep: Gather a bike/sports helmet and a life jacket if available (look for a U.S. Coast Guard–approved label). Read CDC 'HEADS UP' concussion facts and a heat-illness fact sheet.
misconceptions: Thinking you can 'shake off' a head injury. Any suspected concussion means stop playing and tell an adult — 'When in doubt, sit it out.'
Trying to swim straight to shore against a rip current. Swim parallel to shore until out of the current, then swim in (or float and signal for help).

days.guide: Learn drowning prevention (swim with a buddy, only where a lifeguard is on duty, life jackets in boats/open water) and rip currents. Check life-jacket fit: buckle it, lift at the shoulders — it shouldn't ride up past the chin.

questions.q: If caught in a rip current, what should you do?
questions.a: Stay calm, don't fight it; swim parallel to the shore until free, then swim back at an angle — or float and wave/yell for help.

days.guide: Read concussion signs: headache, dizziness, confusion, nausea, blurry vision, light sensitivity, memory problems.

questions.q: What should you do if you hit your head in a game and feel dizzy?
questions.a: Stop playing, tell the coach/parent, and get checked by a health professional before returning.

days.guide: Inspect sports gear; check helmet fit with 2-V-1. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What is the 2-V-1 helmet check?
questions.a: Two fingers above eyebrows, straps form a V under each ear, one finger under the buckled chin strap.

days.guide: Learn heat exhaustion (heavy sweating, cool clammy skin, dizziness, nausea) vs. heat stroke (very high body temperature, confusion, hot skin, fainting — call 911).

questions.q: Which is a medical emergency: heat exhaustion or heat stroke?
questions.a: Heat stroke — call 911 and cool the person immediately.

days.guide: Create a sports safety checklist; take the quiz. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: Name two ways to prevent heat illness.
questions.a: Drink water before/during/after, take breaks in shade, avoid the hottest hours, wear light clothing.

weeks.assessment_key: Checklist: protective gear fitted, water, warm-up, shade breaks, concussion rule, buddy system for water. Quiz key: rip current — swim parallel; life jacket fit; concussion signs and 'sit it out'; 2-V-1; heat exhaustion vs heat stroke (911). Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Gather a bicycle, helmet, and a neighborhood map. California law requires helmets for bicyclists, skateboarders and scooter riders under 18. Cyclists ride with traffic, obey signs and signals, and use lights at night.
misconceptions: Riding against traffic to see cars. Ride in the same direction as traffic so drivers expect you.
Thinking headphones are fine while walking near traffic. They block warning sounds like horns and sirens.

days.guide: Learn CA rules for cyclists and pedestrians. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Which direction should cyclists ride?
questions.a: With traffic, on the right side of the road.

days.guide: Do the ABC quick check (Air, Brakes, Chain) and ride a safe route with a parent. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What does the ABC check stand for?
questions.a: Air (tire pressure), Brakes (working), Chain (oiled, on the gears).

days.guide: Discuss phone and headphone distraction. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Why is texting while walking dangerous?
questions.a: You don't see cars, curbs or obstacles and react more slowly.

days.guide: Analyze stunt videos and peer dares. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Why do stunt videos encourage risky behavior?
questions.a: They show only successes, not injuries, and reward attention with views.

days.guide: Map a safe route and explain hazards. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Name two hazards on a route and how to handle them.
questions.a: Busy intersections (use crosswalks/signals), driveways (watch for backing cars), no sidewalk (walk facing traffic).

weeks.assessment_key: Safe route map: marked route, crosswalks/signals used, at least three hazards labeled with safety strategies. Proficient = all three hazards with strategies.

weeks.prep: Open the home first-aid kit; gather disposable gloves, gauze, bandages and a cold pack. Learn Red Cross Check–Call–Care: Check the scene and the person, Call 911 if needed, Care for the person until help arrives.
misconceptions: Putting ice, butter or toothpaste on a burn. Cool the burn under cool (not ice-cold) running water for about 10 minutes, then cover loosely.
Tilting the head back for a nosebleed. Lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose.

days.guide: Learn Check–Call–Care; practice scene safety checks. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Why check the scene first?
questions.a: So you don't become a second victim (traffic, fire, electricity).

days.guide: Practice direct pressure and bandaging with gloves. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: How do you stop bleeding?
questions.a: Wear gloves, press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth/gauze, and keep pressure; add more gauze on top if blood soaks through.

days.guide: Learn first aid for minor burns and when to get help. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: When does a burn need medical help?
questions.a: If it's large, deep, blistered over a big area, on the face, hands, feet or genitals, or caused by chemicals or electricity.

days.guide: Practice nosebleed care and RICE for sprains. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What does RICE stand for?
questions.a: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation.

days.guide: Inventory and restock the first aid kit; skills check. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Why wear gloves when giving first aid?
questions.a: To protect you and the injured person from germs in blood or body fluids (universal precautions).

weeks.assessment_key: Skills check (✓ each): demonstrates Check–Call–Care, direct pressure and bandage, cool-water burn care, nosebleed (lean forward, pinch), RICE, gloves. Proficient = 5 of 6.

weeks.prep: Find the American Heart Association Hands-Only CPR video and an epinephrine auto-injector trainer video. Use a pillow for practice — never practice thrusts or compressions on a person.
misconceptions: Thinking you should give abdominal thrusts to someone who's coughing hard. If they can cough or speak, encourage coughing; act only if they can't breathe, cough or speak.
Waiting to see if an allergic reaction improves. Signs of anaphylaxis need the epinephrine auto-injector and 911 right away.

days.guide: Learn choking signs (hands at throat, can't speak, cough or breathe) and abdominal-thrust hand position on a pillow (fist above navel, below breastbone).

questions.q: What is the universal sign of choking?
questions.a: Hands clutching the throat.

days.guide: Learn anaphylaxis signs (hives, swelling of lips/tongue/throat, trouble breathing, vomiting) and auto-injector use with a trainer.

questions.q: Where is an epinephrine auto-injector used?
questions.a: Pressed into the outer thigh (through clothing if needed), held for the time stated on the device, and 911 is called.

days.guide: Watch AHA Hands-Only CPR; practice compressions on a pillow to 'Stayin' Alive.' Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What are the two steps of Hands-Only CPR?
questions.a: Call 911, then push hard and fast in the center of the chest (100–120 per minute).

days.guide: Decide in 10 scenarios: call 911, call a parent, or give first aid. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Someone collapses and isn't breathing. What do you do?
questions.a: Call 911 (or have someone call), start Hands-Only CPR, and send someone for an AED if available.

days.guide: Take the Injury Prevention and First Aid unit test. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: Why push to the beat of 'Stayin' Alive'?
questions.a: Its tempo is about 100–120 beats per minute, the right compression rate.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit test key: home hazards and alarms; Poison Control 1-800-222-1222; rip current; concussion; heat stroke = 911; helmet law under 18; Check–Call–Care; direct pressure; burns cool water; RICE; choking signs; anaphylaxis = epinephrine + 911; Hands-Only CPR 100–120/min. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Use a phone that is OFF or unplugged for mock calls (never dial 911 to practice). Make a contact card template. Discuss home-alone rules ahead of time with other caregivers.
misconceptions: Hanging up before the dispatcher says to. Stay on the line and answer questions; the dispatcher may give instructions.
Thinking 911 is for any problem. It's for emergencies where life, health or property is in immediate danger.

days.guide: Learn what dispatchers ask: location, what happened, how many people, is the person breathing. Practice a mock call with you as dispatcher.

questions.q: What is the most important information to give a 911 dispatcher?
questions.a: Your exact location/address, then what the emergency is.

days.guide: Memorize address and parents' numbers; set up an ICE contact. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What is an ICE contact?
questions.a: An 'In Case of Emergency' contact saved in a phone so responders know whom to call.

days.guide: Locate the nearest fire station, hospital and police station on a map. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Why know where the nearest hospital is?
questions.a: So you can get help faster in an emergency.

days.guide: Write home-alone rules with a parent (don't open the door, don't tell callers you're alone, check-in times).

questions.q: If someone knocks while you're home alone, what do you do?
questions.a: Don't open the door; follow family rules and call a parent if worried.

days.guide: Complete the mock-call rubric and contact card. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Should you hang up after giving your address?
questions.a: No — stay on the line until the dispatcher says you can hang up.

weeks.assessment_key: Mock call rubric (✓ each): states address clearly, describes emergency, answers questions calmly, follows instructions, stays on the line. Contact card: address, parent numbers, ICE contact. Proficient = all.

weeks.prep: Graph paper and a flashlight. Read the Great ShakeOut 'Drop, Cover, and Hold On' guidance and NFPA home fire escape planning tips. Check that smoke alarms work.
misconceptions: Running outside during an earthquake. Drop, cover and hold on where you are; falling objects near buildings are dangerous.
Standing in a doorway during an earthquake. Modern doorways aren't stronger; get under a sturdy table instead.

days.guide: Review why California has earthquakes (Pacific and North American plates sliding past along faults like the San Andreas) and what to do indoors, outdoors and in a car.

questions.q: What should you do if an earthquake hits while you're in a car?
questions.a: Pull over away from buildings, trees, overpasses and power lines, set the brake and stay inside until shaking stops.

days.guide: Practice Drop, Cover and Hold On in 3 rooms; identify safe spots. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What are the steps of Drop, Cover and Hold On?
questions.a: Drop to hands and knees, cover your head and neck under a sturdy table, hold on until shaking stops.

days.guide: Draw a home floor plan with two exits from each room and a meeting place. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Why have two exits from each room?
questions.a: If one exit is blocked by fire or smoke, you can use the other.

days.guide: Run a family fire drill and time it; practice stop, drop and roll and crawling low. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Why crawl low in a fire?
questions.a: Smoke and heat rise; cleaner air is near the floor.

days.guide: Quiz on earthquake and fire safety. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: What is an aftershock?
questions.a: A smaller earthquake that follows the main one.

weeks.assessment_key: Escape plan: floor plan with two exits per room, outside meeting place, alarms marked. Quiz key: Drop, Cover, Hold On; car response; aftershocks; crawl low; feel doors with back of hand; stop, drop and roll; test smoke alarms monthly. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Print the Ready.gov emergency kit checklist and family communication plan. Get a backpack. Look up your county's evacuation zone system (e.g., Genasys Protect) and AirNow.gov for AQI. AQI colors: green 0–50 good, yellow 51–100 moderate, orange 101–150 unhealthy for sensitive groups, red 151–200 unhealthy, purple 201–300 very unhealthy, maroon 301+ hazardous.
misconceptions: Waiting for an evacuation order to start packing. Have a go-bag ready ahead of time and leave when told.
Thinking any mask blocks smoke. Cloth masks don't filter fine smoke particles; well-fitted N95 masks do.

days.guide: Learn evacuation zones and read the AQI. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: The AQI is 165. What should you do?
questions.a: It's 'unhealthy' (red): stay indoors, close windows, limit outdoor activity, and use an air purifier if available.

days.guide: Pack or list a 72-hour go-bag. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: How much water should a go-bag plan for?
questions.a: About one gallon per person per day, for at least three days.

days.guide: Complete a family communication plan with an out-of-area contact. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Why have an out-of-area contact?
questions.a: Local phone lines may be overloaded; family members can all check in with one person far away.

days.guide: Plan how to help a neighbor, pet or elderly relative. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: How can you prepare to help a pet in an emergency?
questions.a: Pack food, water, leash/carrier, medications and vaccination records in the go-bag.

days.guide: Present the family plan; take the Preparedness quiz. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: Name five items for a go-bag.
questions.a: Water, non-perishable food, flashlight, batteries, first aid kit, medications, phone charger, N95 masks, copies of documents, cash.

weeks.assessment_key: Family plan: meeting places, out-of-area contact, go-bag list, pet/neighbor plan. Quiz key: AQI levels; go-bag contents; 1 gallon/person/day; N95 for smoke; evacuation zones; Drop, Cover, Hold On; fire escape. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Write scenario cards for warning signs and de-escalation. PARENT PREVIEW: this week discusses weapons and gangs; decide how to discuss any firearms in your home and how they are stored.
misconceptions: Thinking violence is only physical. Verbal threats and emotional abuse are violence too.
Thinking you should handle a weapon to make it safe. Never touch it — leave and tell an adult.

days.guide: Discuss physical, verbal and emotional violence and effects. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Give an example of emotional violence.
questions.a: Threats, constant insults, humiliation or controlling someone through fear.

days.guide: List warning signs of potential violence (threats, talk of weapons, uncontrolled anger, posting threats online) and why to tell an adult.

questions.q: If a classmate posts a threat online, what should you do?
questions.a: Take it seriously, screenshot it, and tell a trusted adult or school official right away.

days.guide: Learn the rule if you see a gun: don't touch, leave the area, tell an adult. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What three steps do you follow if you find a gun?
questions.a: Don't touch it, leave the area, tell an adult right away.

days.guide: Read about gang recruitment (promises of belonging, protection, money) and list positive alternatives.

questions.q: Name two positive alternatives to gangs.
questions.a: Sports teams, clubs, youth groups, volunteering, mentoring programs, jobs/arts programs.

days.guide: Role-play de-escalating a heated argument; complete the check. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Name two de-escalation strategies.
questions.a: Stay calm, speak softly, give space, listen, avoid insults, walk away and get an adult.

weeks.assessment_key: Role-play rubric: 4 = calm voice, gives space, listens, uses I-messages, walks away/gets help if needed; 3 = most; 2 = some; 1 = escalates. Check key: types of violence; warning signs; don't touch-leave-tell; gang alternatives.

weeks.prep: Write scenario cards for 'uh-oh' feelings, boundaries and grooming warning signs. Choose a family code word. PARENT PREVIEW: grooming and unwanted touch are discussed; reassure your child they can always tell you, and that it is never a child's fault.
misconceptions: Thinking abusers are always strangers. Most people who harm children are people they know; warning signs matter more than who the person is.
Thinking you must obey every adult. You can say no to anything that feels unsafe, even to adults you know.

days.guide: Discuss intuition; identify 'uh-oh' feelings in scenarios. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: What should you do when something gives you an 'uh-oh' feeling?
questions.a: Trust it, get away from the situation, and tell a trusted adult.

days.guide: Learn personal-boundary rights; practice saying no to unwanted touch or requests. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What is consent?
questions.a: Freely given permission; you have the right to say no to touch or requests, and others must respect it.

days.guide: Learn grooming warning signs: secrets, special gifts, isolating you, testing boundaries, online flattery.

questions.q: An adult gives you gifts and says, 'Don't tell your parents.' Is that a warning sign?
questions.a: Yes — secrets and gifts are grooming warning signs; tell a trusted adult right away.

days.guide: Practice No-Go-Tell and create a family code word. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What does No-Go-Tell mean?
questions.a: Say no, get away, and tell a trusted adult.

days.guide: Take the Violence Prevention and Personal Safety unit quiz. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: What is a family code word used for?
questions.a: A secret word you or a trusted ride must know, or a signal to ask to be picked up when you feel unsafe.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit quiz key: types of violence; warning signs; gun rule (don't touch, leave, tell); gang alternatives; de-escalation; boundaries and consent; grooming signs (secrets, gifts, isolation); No-Go-Tell; code word; never the child's fault. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Toothbrush, floss, a hygiene checklist, and KidsHealth articles on acne and hygiene. Gather a sports bag to talk about gear hygiene.
misconceptions: Thinking acne comes from dirt or chocolate. Acne mainly comes from hormones increasing oil that clogs pores with dead skin and bacteria.
Thinking bleeding gums mean you should stop flossing. Bleeding is a sign of gingivitis; gentle daily flossing helps gums heal.

days.guide: Review skin, hair and body odor care; update the routine. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Why does body odor increase in middle school?
questions.a: Puberty hormones activate sweat glands; bacteria break down sweat and cause odor.

days.guide: Sort acne myths and facts; plan a gentle skin routine. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Should you pop pimples?
questions.a: No — popping can spread bacteria, cause infection and scars.

days.guide: Learn about gingivitis; practice proper flossing (C-shape around each tooth, below the gumline).

questions.q: What is gingivitis?
questions.a: Early gum disease from plaque buildup; signs are red, swollen, bleeding gums.

days.guide: List sports hygiene rules (shower after practice, wash uniforms, don't share towels, dry feet, wear flip-flops in locker rooms).

questions.q: How do you prevent athlete's foot?
questions.a: Keep feet clean and dry, change socks, wear sandals in locker rooms, don't share towels.

days.guide: Complete a hygiene self-assessment and quiz. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: How often should you brush and floss?
questions.a: Brush twice a day for two minutes; floss once a day.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: hormones cause more sweat/oil; acne myths; gingivitis signs; brush 2×2, floss daily; athlete's foot prevention; deodorant vs antiperspirant. Self-assessment complete and honest. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Print a 3-night sleep log. Install a free sound meter app. Get a sunscreen bottle. Know: preteens 6–12 need 9–12 hours of sleep (13–18: 8–10); the 60/60 rule for headphones (no more than 60% volume for 60 minutes at a time); prolonged noise above about 85 decibels can damage hearing; 20-20-20 eye rule.
misconceptions: Thinking you can catch up on all lost sleep on weekends. Sleep debt builds up; regular schedules work best.
Thinking sunscreen is only for beach days. UV rays reach you on cloudy days and in everyday outdoor time.

days.guide: Learn why 9–12 hours matter; keep a 3-night sleep log. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Name two effects of sleep debt.
questions.a: Trouble concentrating, irritability, weaker immune system, slower reaction time.

days.guide: Discuss blue light and phones in bedrooms; plan a device curfew. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Why can screens before bed disturb sleep?
questions.a: Blue light and stimulating content delay the release of melatonin and keep the brain alert.

days.guide: Measure common noises with the app; learn the 60/60 rule. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: What is the 60/60 rule?
questions.a: Listen at no more than 60% volume for no more than 60 minutes at a time.

days.guide: Read a sunscreen label (SPF 30+, broad spectrum, reapply every 2 hours); check the UV index; learn 20-20-20.

questions.q: What is the 20-20-20 rule?
questions.a: Every 20 minutes of screen time, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds.

days.guide: Write a personal health practice goal; take the quiz. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: What does 'broad spectrum' mean on sunscreen?
questions.a: It protects against both UVA and UVB rays.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 9–12 hours sleep; sleep debt; blue light; 60/60 rule; 85 dB; SPF 30+ broad spectrum, reapply every 2 hours; 20-20-20. Goal: SMART and tied to sleep, hearing, sun or eye health.

weeks.prep: Gather glitter (or flour), soap, a timer. Prepare a chart: bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa.
misconceptions: Thinking antibiotics cure colds and flu. Antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses.
Thinking a quick water rinse cleans hands. Scrub with soap for at least 20 seconds.

days.guide: Compare pathogens and give examples. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Give a disease caused by a virus, a bacterium, a fungus and a protozoan.
questions.a: Virus: flu, cold, COVID-19; bacterium: strep throat; fungus: athlete's foot/ringworm; protozoan: malaria or giardia.

days.guide: Model germ spread with glitter on hands and objects. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What did the glitter show?
questions.a: Germs spread easily from hands to objects and other people.

days.guide: Test glitter removal: water only vs. 20-second soap wash. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: Why does soap work better than water alone?
questions.a: Soap breaks up oils and lifts germs off skin so they rinse away.

days.guide: Draw lines of defense: skin and mucus, white blood cells, antibodies; explain vaccines. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: How does a vaccine protect you?
questions.a: It shows the immune system a harmless form or piece of a germ, so the body makes antibodies and memory cells ready to fight the real germ.

days.guide: Communicable disease quiz. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: Are antibiotics effective against viruses?
questions.a: No — they only work on bacteria.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: four pathogen types with examples; spread by contact, droplets, contaminated food/water, vectors; handwashing 20 seconds; lines of defense; antibodies; vaccines; antibiotics only for bacteria. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Print a simple family health history form (CDC 'My Family Health Portrait' has one). Find kid-friendly sources on asthma, diabetes, heart disease and cancer (KidsHealth, CDC). PARENT PREVIEW: decide what family health information you're comfortable sharing.
misconceptions: Thinking chronic diseases only affect old people. Asthma and type 1 diabetes often start in childhood, and habits now affect later risk.
Thinking you can 'catch' diabetes or asthma. Noncommunicable diseases aren't spread from person to person.

days.guide: Your child researches one chronic disease and makes a fact card (what it is, symptoms, risk factors, prevention/treatment).

questions.q: What makes a disease 'chronic' and 'noncommunicable'?
questions.a: It lasts a long time (or for life) and can't be spread from person to person.

days.guide: Learn asthma triggers (pollen, dust, smoke, pets, cold air, exercise) and how a quick-relief inhaler opens airways; discuss helping a friend (help them sit up, use their inhaler, get an adult, call 911 if severe).

questions.q: What does a quick-relief (rescue) inhaler do?
questions.a: It relaxes the muscles around the airways so they open and breathing is easier.

days.guide: Sort controllable (diet, activity, smoking, sleep) and uncontrollable (age, genetics, family history) risk factors.

questions.q: Is family history controllable or uncontrollable?
questions.a: Uncontrollable — but knowing it helps you focus on controllable habits.

days.guide: Complete a simple family health history with a parent. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Why is a family health history useful?
questions.a: It shows which diseases run in the family so doctors can check for them and you can lower your risk.

days.guide: Write a paragraph on habits that lower chronic disease risk; complete the check. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Name three habits that lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes.
questions.a: Regular physical activity, eating plenty of fruits/vegetables/whole grains, limiting sugary drinks, not smoking or vaping, getting enough sleep.

weeks.assessment_key: Check key: chronic vs. communicable; type 1 diabetes = body makes little/no insulin; type 2 = body doesn't use insulin well; asthma triggers and inhaler; controllable vs uncontrollable risk factors. Paragraph rubric: 4 = three or more specific habits linked to specific diseases; 3 = habits without links; 2 = one habit; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Gather two versions (name-brand and generic/store-brand) of a product like shampoo, toothpaste or sunscreen with price tags. Find 4 health-product ads. Unit price = price ÷ number of units (ounces).
misconceptions: Thinking name brands are always better. Generic products often have the same active ingredients for less money.
Believing testimonials prove a product works. Personal stories aren't scientific evidence.

days.guide: Analyze 4 health-product ads for claims, techniques and missing information. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What questions should you ask about an ad claim?
questions.a: Who says so? What evidence? What's left out? Who profits?

days.guide: Compare name-brand and generic by ingredients and unit price. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: A 10-oz bottle costs $5.00 and a 16-oz bottle costs $6.40. Which is the better unit price?
questions.a: The 16-oz bottle: $0.40 per ounce vs. $0.50 per ounce.

days.guide: Identify red flags of health fraud (miracle cure, secret formula, testimonials only, 'act now').

questions.q: What is quackery?
questions.a: Selling health products or treatments that don't work, using false or unproven claims.
