days.guide: Use DECIDE to choose a sunscreen or toothpaste and justify. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What should you look for in a toothpaste?
questions.a: Fluoride and the ADA Seal of Acceptance.

days.guide: Complete the consumer-health worksheet. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What is a generic product?
questions.a: A product without a brand name, usually with the same active ingredients and lower price.

weeks.assessment_key: Worksheet key: identifies ad techniques and missing info; computes unit prices correctly; names three quackery red flags; justifies a product choice using ingredients, evidence and price. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: With a parent, look at family health records (immunization record, last check-up). Have a prescription label example. Look up a local clinic, dentist and the county public health department online.
misconceptions: Thinking you only see a doctor when sick. Regular check-ups catch problems early and keep vaccines current.
Being afraid to ask a doctor or pharmacist questions. Asking questions is your right and keeps you safe.

days.guide: Match 10 providers to what they do (pediatrician, dentist, orthodontist, optometrist, dermatologist, pharmacist, school nurse, counselor, allergist, physical therapist).

questions.q: What does a dermatologist treat?
questions.a: Skin, hair and nail conditions (like acne).

days.guide: Write questions for the next check-up; learn what a well-child visit includes (growth, vision, hearing, vaccines, questions).

questions.q: Name three things checked at a well-child visit.
questions.a: Height and weight, blood pressure, vision and hearing, vaccines, development and questions about health.

days.guide: Read a prescription label; list questions for a pharmacist. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: What should you ask a pharmacist about a new medicine?
questions.a: How and when to take it, side effects, whether to take it with food, and interactions with other medicines.

days.guide: Locate a local clinic, dentist and public health department. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What does a public health department do?
questions.a: Protects community health: vaccines, disease tracking, food safety, health education.

days.guide: Take the Personal and Consumer Health unit test. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: What is a specialist?
questions.a: A doctor with extra training in one area (e.g., allergist, dermatologist).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit test key: hygiene and gingivitis; sleep needs; 60/60 rule; sunscreen; pathogens; vaccines; antibiotics only for bacteria; chronic disease risk factors; asthma; unit price; quackery; health-care providers. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Bookmark AirNow.gov for daily AQI. Print a trash audit sheet (categories: recyclable, compostable, landfill). Find your county public health department website.
misconceptions: Thinking environmental health is someone else's job. Individual and family choices affect air, water and waste.
Thinking clear water is always safe. Unsafe water can look clear; public systems test it.

days.guide: Check the local AQI daily for a week and graph it. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What color and number range is 'good' air quality?
questions.a: Green, 0–50.

days.guide: Learn about safe drinking water (testing, boil-water notices) and noise pollution. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: What is a boil-water notice?
questions.a: An alert that tap water may be contaminated; boil it before drinking or cooking.

days.guide: Conduct a one-day household trash audit; plan reduce/reuse/recycle steps. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Which is most effective: reduce, reuse or recycle?
questions.a: Reduce — creating less waste in the first place.

days.guide: Research what your county public health department does. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Name two services of a county public health department.
questions.a: Vaccination clinics, disease tracking, restaurant inspections, health education, emergency preparedness.

days.guide: Choose a community health issue for the advocacy project and justify it. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What makes a good advocacy topic?
questions.a: It affects many people, has a clear healthy action, and can be supported with facts.

weeks.assessment_key: Project proposal: names a community health issue, explains why it matters with at least one fact, identifies an audience, and proposes a healthy action. Proficient = all four.

weeks.prep: Gather poster paper, computer, camera. Print an advocacy rubric: clear message, accurate facts from valid sources (cited), audience fit, persuasive design, call to action, presentation delivery.
misconceptions: Using facts without sources. Every fact should be cited from a valid source.
Leaving out a call to action. Audiences need a specific action.

days.guide: Gather 4 facts from valid sources. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Name two valid sources for your topic.
questions.a: CDC.gov, Ready.gov, AirNow.gov, KidsHealth, county public health department.

days.guide: Identify audience, message and call to action. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Give an example of a call to action.
questions.a: 'Check your smoke alarms this weekend!'

days.guide: Produce a poster, brochure, slide show or video. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: How can design make the message more persuasive?
questions.a: Clear headlines, strong images, simple facts and a bold call to action.

days.guide: Practice a 3-minute presentation; get feedback. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What makes a presentation effective?
questions.a: Eye contact, clear voice, accurate facts and a confident call to action.

days.guide: Revise using the rubric. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why revise before presenting?
questions.a: To fix weak areas the rubric or feedback revealed.

weeks.assessment_key: Advocacy rubric (1–4 each): clear health-enhancing message; at least 4 accurate, cited facts; audience fit; persuasive design; call to action. Proficient = 3+ each.

weeks.prep: Arrange an audience (family, co-op, community group). Prepare a review game on mental health, safety and personal health. Print the end-of-year assessment and the week 1 wellness wheel.
misconceptions: Thinking health learning ends with the course. Skills like decision making and communication are used for life.
Thinking summer means no safety planning. Water, heat, sun and bike safety matter most in summer.

days.guide: Present the advocacy project. Set up a simple 'stage' and audience, have your child introduce the work, and hold applause until the end; afterward ask them to name one strength and one thing to improve before you add one specific comment.

questions.q: What was your call to action?
questions.a: Answer varies; should be specific.

days.guide: Play the review game. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Name three steps of DECIDE.
questions.a: Any three of: Define, Explore, Consider, Identify values, Decide, Evaluate.

days.guide: Take the end-of-year assessment. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What number do you call or text for mental health crisis support?

days.guide: Re-rate the wellness wheel and compare with week 1. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Which area improved most and why?
questions.a: Answer varies; should cite specific habits.

days.guide: Write a reflection and summer health and safety plan. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Name two summer safety practices.
questions.a: Sunscreen SPF 30+, swimming with a buddy/life jacket, helmet when biking, hydration in heat.

weeks.assessment_key: Final assessment key: wellness dimensions; DECIDE; CRAAP; stress response and coping; I-messages; conflict steps; bullying definition; stop-screenshot-block-tell; 988; Check–Call–Care; Hands-Only CPR; Drop, Cover, Hold On; go-bag; gun safety rule; No-Go-Tell; pathogens and vaccines; unit price. Presentation rubric as in week 35. Proficient = 80%.
